name: Writing an Executive Brief
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: One Page, No Nonsense: Writing an Executive Brief on Quantum Computing
lesson.summary: An executive brief distills a complex, uncertain technical topic into a short document a decision maker can actually use, stating clearly what is known, what is uncertain, and what action, if any, is warranted right now, without either alarmism or false reassurance.
lesson.body:
An executive brief is written for a specific kind of reader: someone with limited time, who is not a technical specialist in the subject, and who needs to make or inform a real decision, a budget choice, a policy position, a security posture. That constraint should shape everything about how it is written. It should be short, often literally one page. It should front load the conclusion rather than build up to it gradually. And it should separate fact from interpretation from recommendation clearly enough that a busy reader cannot accidentally blur the three together.

A workable structure for a quantum computing brief draws directly on earlier chapters as its actual source material. Start with a single line stating the bottom line up front, what the reader should take away and do, if anything. Follow with a short section on what is known, grounded in verified, replicated results, this is where technology due diligence and its Technology Readiness Level discipline feeds in directly, state plainly what maturity level the relevant claims are actually at rather than borrowing the confident language of a press release. Follow with a short section on what remains uncertain, this is where each breakthrough is uncertain and the field's general base rate track record belong, stated honestly rather than hedged into meaninglessness. Close with a short recommendation section built on the risk assessment framework, likelihood multiplied by impact, rather than on how alarming the underlying claim happens to sound.

A concrete mini example shows the structure at work, using two claims already covered in this course: the threat to current encryption from quantum computers is real but overstated on any near term timeline, and quantum computers augment classical computing for specific problem types, they do not replace it. A good brief states both plainly and specifically. For example: near term risk is low, but data with long confidentiality requirements is already exposed to future decryption under a harvest now, decrypt later attack, so migrating to post quantum cryptographic standards on a normal, multi year infrastructure timeline is the prudent, unpanicked action. That framing avoids the two most common failure modes in badly written technology briefs, dismissing the topic entirely or inflating it into an urgent crisis, both of which are equally unhelpful to a reader trying to make a real decision.

A few closing craft notes make the difference between a brief that holds up and one that does not. Write findings as specific, falsifiable statements rather than vague adjectives, say no fault tolerant, error corrected quantum computer capable of running Shor's algorithm at cryptographically relevant scale has been publicly demonstrated, not the technology isn't ready yet. Cite what a claim is actually based on, a peer reviewed, replicated result versus a company announcement, since that distinction is exactly what technology due diligence and Bayesian reasoning trained you to notice. And always keep what you know separate from what you recommend, so a reader who disagrees with your judgment call can still trust that your facts are solid.
